title: AI-assisted euthanasia? New film addresses prospect of care robots
summary: While the world debates the dangers of artificial intelligence, filmmaker Doris Dörrie explores how humanoid robots could change the way we deal with aging, caregiving and how people choose to die.

image.caption: A care robot named Pavlovich takes over the care of Mrs. WinklerImage: Mathias Bothor/Zeitsprung Pictures/Wild Bunch Germany/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hamburg in the near future: Instead of delivery drivers, robots deliver parcels. In cafés, talking and serving robots roll between the tables. On the streets, one encounters humanoid robots walking dogs — or the other way around, people taking their robot dogs for a walk.

This is the setting of Doris Dörrie's new film, "Frau Winkler verlässt das Haus" ("Mrs. Winkler Leaves the House"). At the core of the plot is an elderly woman who can no longer live on her own after a fall. With her only daughter unable to provide permanent care, the solution seems simple enough: a care robot with a built-in EOL program, or "End of Life" mode. This robot not only assists with everyday life but can also provide assisted dying under certain conditions, namely when the person explicitly wishes to end their life and meets the relevant medical criteria.

Dörrie's film tackles several major social issues with remarkable lightness. These include the challenges facing ageing societies such as Germany, Japan and China, the question of dying on one's own terms and a mother-daughter relationship that raises questions of guilt and responsibility. Even though the story is set in Germany, such issues resonate globally.
"I write about what personally moves and interests me," Dörrie tells DW.

One of the best-known contemporary German film directors, Doris Dörrie achieved her breakthrough in 1985 with the comedy "Men…," and later gained international recognition with films such as "Cherry Blossoms" and "Greetings from Fukushima."
Who decides when we die?

Assisted suicide is one of the most complex ethical questions of our time. Laws vary considerably around the world. While some countries permit active euthanasia under certain conditions, others prohibit and criminalize all forms of assisted suicide.
What is assisted suicide and where does Germany stand?
In her film, Doris Dörrie asks what happens when AI begins calculating the cost of caring for an elderly person and weighing whether that cost is still "worth" bearing for society.

But the underlying idea isn't new, Dörrie says, pointing to the Japanese legend of Narayama, which is also mentioned in the film. According to the legend, the eldest children were responsible for taking their ageing parents to a mountain and leaving them there to die because there was not enough food for everyone. "And that's also the debate we are currently facing to a certain extent: Can we really afford to let older people live longer and longer?"

In Dörrie's film, elderly people are allowed to make their own decisions once they reach a certain state of health, but they can't change their minds afterwards. Yet what does it really mean to make a decision freely? "It's a tricky situation," says Dörrie, because the question is to what extent one is also pressured into making this decision, "not only because it makes more economic sense, but also because one is no longer a burden on one's loved ones — in this case, one's daughter..."

The film often raises these questions indirectly and with plenty of dark humor. At one point, a care adviser presents the EOL feature to Mrs. Winkler as an attractive and, above all, straightforward additional option, making it sound as though there would be nothing more for her to worry about.

blocks.caption: Doris Dörrie (left) with actors Angela Winkler and Laura TonkeImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Staying close despite the algorithm

Dörrie is not interested in demonizing AI in her film — quite the opposite. In the film, the care robot, which Mrs. Winkler names Pavlovich, helps the elderly woman rediscover some of her zest for life and get out of the house.

"When you travel through Germany, you see small houses everywhere," Dörrie says, "and statistics show that an elderly person lives alone in every other house. If AI can help in these circumstances, why not use it?" The filmmaker says it's precisely this ambiguity she wants to explore in her film. Dividing things into black and white would neither be interesting nor, in her view, accurate.

Dörrie and her film crew were also surprised during filming by how quickly people can develop an emotional bond with a robot. She attributes this to the human brain. "We regard anything that moves and speaks as a living being. We can't help it," she explains. And that is precisely what we need to pay attention to when interacting with AI, Dörrie says. "How often are we truly aware that we are talking to a machine rather than a living being? These are things we still have to learn."
How robots are helping solve China's elderly care crisis
The difference between humans and machines

Looking at the development of AI, it seems that the boundaries between humans and machines are becoming increasingly blurred. That is precisely why we need to talk about it, Doris Dörrie says. In her view, things become problematic "when we can no longer distance ourselves from technology and stop forming our own thoughts."

As human beings, we need to ask ourselves who we are and what truly defines us, Dörrie says. "I believe there is a major difference between robots and us, and that is the ability to play. A robot might be able to initiate a game, she explains, "but play itself is something profoundly human because it has no particular meaning or purpose."

Alongside these philosophical questions about what it means to be human, the filmmaker also makes a clear call for AI regulation: "At some point, we had to discuss nuclear weapons internationally, too. We've talked about all kinds of issues in the past, and we haven't just talked about them — we've also managed to find solutions," she points out.
She says this is something that urgently needs to be addressed. "And I believe we need to move very quickly on this, too."
This article was originally written in German.
